original_review_text:
This proposal addresses an important and timely problem: how to integrate public spatial transcriptomic and spatial proteomic datasets to infer cell state from molecular abundance and subcellular organization. The central premise, that spatial organization of RNA and protein contains information beyond abundance-only summaries, is compelling and well aligned with current needs in spatial omics. The proposed framework combines non-rigid registration, rasterization to matched spatial patches, extraction of interpretable spatial features, and RNA-to-protein predictive modeling. If successful, it could provide a useful community resource for cross-modal spatial omics analysis and help shift the field from descriptive cell typing toward predictive models of cellular organization.

The strongest aspects are the focus on public data synthesis, the use of a defined validation resource in Spatch, the attempt to benchmark spatial models against abundance-only and spatially shuffled controls, and the commitment to open-source, containerized workflows. The use of diffeomorphic registration and patch-based harmonization is technically appropriate for adjacent-section spatial datasets, and the evaluation plan includes several sensible metrics, including landmark error, molecular concordance, deformation regularity, and negative controls. The project clearly requires expertise across spatial omics, image registration, machine learning, statistical validation, and cell biology, and the requested NCEMS support for data harmonization, computation, and project coordination is plausible.

However, the proposal is stronger as a computational framework project than as a definitive biological test of cell fate emergence. The first two activities are reasonably well grounded in identifiable public datasets, especially Spatch, but Activity 3 is underdeveloped. The proposal does not clearly identify the trajectory or lineage datasets to be used, nor does it establish that public datasets exist with the necessary spatial transcriptomic, spatial proteomic, and fate information to test whether biophysical fingerprints precede fate decisions. In its current form, the cell fate hypothesis risks becoming speculative or dependent on inferred pseudotime rather than experimentally grounded fate outcomes. The proposal also sometimes conflates adjacent-section correspondence with true subcellular one-to-one molecular correspondence; even excellent registration cannot fully resolve section-to-section biological differences, segmentation uncertainty, or the fact that RNA and protein measurements may come from different cells in adjacent slices. These limitations should be more explicitly modeled and propagated into downstream prediction uncertainty.

The machine learning plan is promising but not fully specified. The contrastive embedding and RNA-to-protein predictor are described at a high level, but the proposal does not provide sufficient detail on model architectures, sample splitting strategies, cross-tissue generalization, leakage prevention beyond shuffling controls, uncertainty quantification, or how performance will be interpreted biologically. Given the terabyte-scale imaging data and high-dimensional features, rigorous train/test separation across patients, tissue regions, and cancer types will be essential. The proposal would also benefit from clearer definitions of the proposed 'biophysical fingerprint': which dimensions are mechanistic, which are learned latent variables, and how they will be distinguished from batch, tissue morphology, or staining artifacts. There is also a potential compliance ambiguity in the statement that one investigator will provide single-molecule models and measurements to inform constraints; the funding call prohibits generation of new experimental data, so the proposal should clarify that no new measurements will be generated.

Overall, this is a scientifically significant and technically relevant synthesis proposal with a strong fit to public spatial omics integration and open tool development. Its main weakness is that the biological claims, especially regarding prediction of cell fate decisions, exceed the specificity of the available data and analysis plan. I would view it as a strong proposal if framed primarily as a rigorous, open benchmark and synthesis framework for cross-modal spatial RNA-protein prediction, with more cautious and better-defined downstream biological applications.

While the technical workflow and commitment to open-source benchmarking are commendable, the downstream biological applications regarding cell fate prediction lack specificity and experimental grounding. Overall, the project represents a strong data synthesis and cross-modal prediction resource, provided the scope is focused on computational modeling rather than speculative biological claims.

original_review_text:
This proposal addresses an important and timely problem: how to synthesize spatial transcriptomic and spatial proteomic datasets to infer cell-state information beyond abundance measurements. The central idea, that subcellular RNA and protein localization encode biophysical cell states not captured by conventional count-based analyses, is compelling and well aligned with the call's interest in emergence phenomena in molecular and cellular biosciences. The proposed framework combines existing spatial registration, rasterization, feature extraction, contrastive multimodal learning, and RNA-to-protein prediction, with public paired spatial datasets as the core resource. The plan is technically plausible in parts and includes sensible benchmarks and controls, including abundance-only baselines, spatial shuffles, landmark-based registration metrics, and inverse-consistency checks. The commitment to open code, containerized workflows, harmonized datasets, and public model releases is also strong.

However, the proposal overstates some aspects of what can be inferred from the available data. Adjacent-section registration can align tissue structures, but it cannot truly establish one-to-one subcellular correspondence between RNA and protein in the same cell or subcellular compartment. This is a critical limitation for claims about subcellular localization, cell fate prediction, and RNA-to-protein localization mapping. The proposal acknowledges adjacent sections but then repeatedly describes matched subcellular patches and per-cell protein-localization prediction in ways that may exceed the resolution and biological comparability of the data. The second hypothesis on cell fate is particularly underdeveloped: the trajectory or lineage datasets are not specified, it is unclear whether they include paired public spatial RNA/protein data, and inferred trajectories from static public data are unlikely to demonstrate that fingerprints 'precede' fate decisions without strong temporal or lineage information. The 'Application Set' is left vague, making feasibility difficult to assess. The machine learning plan also lacks sufficient detail on model architecture, uncertainty estimation, train/test partitioning by patient/tissue/platform, prevention of spatial leakage, handling of batch effects, and biological interpretability. The proposal would be strengthened by narrowing its claims to cross-modal spatial prediction and benchmarking, explicitly treating adjacent-section mismatch as a major source of uncertainty, and defining the application datasets and success criteria more concretely.

Overall, this is a strong concept for a community-scale synthesis project, with a useful open computational product likely to result if well executed. Its main weaknesses are overambitious biological claims, insufficiently specified public datasets beyond Spatch, and some methodological ambiguity around what constitutes true subcellular correspondence and cell-fate prediction.

original_review_text:
This proposal addresses an important and timely problem: how to integrate public spatial transcriptomic and proteomic datasets to move beyond abundance-centric definitions of cell state. The proposed framework of image registration, rasterization onto shared patches, extraction of spatial/biophysical features, and cross-modal prediction is well aligned with the call’s emphasis on synthesis of existing public molecular and cellular data. The project has several appealing aspects, including the use of an identified public paired spatial RNA/protein resource, explicit benchmarking against abundance-only baselines, attention to negative controls for spatial leakage, and a commitment to releasing code, models, and harmonized datasets.

The strongest scientific premise is Hypothesis 1: that spatial organization of RNA and protein contains information about cell state not captured by abundance alone. The proposal articulates reasonable computational tests of this idea using paired Xenium/CosMx and CODEX data, and it proposes metrics for registration accuracy, patch correspondence, and predictive performance. The use of existing tools such as STalign and SEraster improves feasibility. If successful, the resulting workflow could be useful to the spatial omics community and could provide a platform for more interpretable cross-modal analyses.

However, the proposal is less convincing in its biological ambition than in its computational workflow. The most serious concern is the assumption that adjacent tissue sections can support subcellular one-to-one correspondence of RNA and protein localization. Even with high-quality diffeomorphic alignment, adjacent sections generally do not contain the same exact cells or subcellular structures. This makes claims about subcellular RNA-protein relationships, protein localization prediction, and biophysical fingerprints potentially vulnerable to confounding by tissue architecture, cell type composition, or neighborhood structure rather than true matched subcellular organization. The proposal acknowledges registration challenges and includes useful controls, but it does not fully address the biological limits of adjacent-section matching.

A second major weakness is that Hypothesis 2, involving prediction of cell fate decisions, is underdeveloped and insufficiently supported by the identified data. The proposal refers to trajectory datasets and progenitor-to-differentiated transitions, but the specific public datasets, modalities, compatibility with the proposed RNA/protein framework, and availability of fate information are not clearly defined. In the absence of true lineage tracing, temporal sampling, or validated fate annotations, it will be difficult to distinguish prediction of future fate from reconstruction of known cell identity or pseudotime. This aim risks overextending the framework beyond what the available public data can support.

The project is clearly a synthesis effort and has a credible rationale for NCEMS support, especially for harmonizing large imaging datasets and providing scalable compute. Nevertheless, the proposal would be stronger with a more concrete inventory of all datasets, a narrower and better validated biological question, clearer definitions of the proposed “biophysical fingerprint,” and more explicit plans for trainee involvement and community engagement. Overall, this is a strong methodological synthesis proposal with good potential impact, but its claims about subcellular correspondence and fate prediction need substantial refinement.

original_review_text:
This proposal addresses an important and timely problem: how to synthesize emerging public spatial transcriptomic and proteomic datasets to infer cell state from molecular abundance and subcellular organization. The conceptual premise is strong. As in protein interaction and regulatory networks, cellular phenotypes often emerge from relationships among components rather than from component abundance alone; therefore, a framework that explicitly models spatial RNA-protein correspondence, membrane/nuclear localization, polarity, and local density could provide meaningful new insight into cell state regulation. The proposed pipeline combines existing tools for diffeomorphic registration and rasterization with downstream contrastive embedding and RNA-to-protein prediction, and it is well aligned with the call's emphasis on public-data synthesis, reusable workflows, and community-scale infrastructure. The Spatch paired Xenium/CosMx-CODEX cancer atlas is an appropriate validation resource, and the plan to release code, models, harmonized datasets, and containerized workflows is a clear strength.

The proposal is strongest as a methods and synthesis infrastructure project. It identifies a real bottleneck in the field: spatial RNA and protein measurements are increasingly available, but cross-modal integration at subcellular or near-subcellular resolution remains difficult, particularly for adjacent tissue sections. The evaluation plan includes sensible quantitative metrics for registration quality, deformation regularity, mask overlap, molecular concordance, and negative controls such as spatial shuffling. The abundance-only and non-spatial baselines are also appropriate and directly test the central hypothesis that spatial organization adds information beyond expression levels.

However, several aspects weaken the scientific rigor and feasibility. First, the proposal sometimes overstates what can be inferred from adjacent-section public data. True subcellular one-to-one RNA-protein correspondence is difficult when RNA and protein are measured in serial sections rather than the same physical cells. Registration can align tissue architecture, but it cannot fully resolve cell-to-cell or subcellular differences across sections, especially in heterogeneous tumors. The proposal acknowledges registration challenges but does not sufficiently discuss how uncertainty in alignment will propagate into the learned fingerprints and predictive models. Second, the cell fate aim is underdeveloped. The Spatch cancer atlas can support cell-state analysis, but cell fate prediction requires datasets with lineage, temporal, perturbational, or developmental structure. The proposed 'Application Set' is not adequately specified, and it is unclear which public paired spatial RNA/protein datasets contain the information needed to distinguish early fate determinants from correlated differences among cell types. Without clearer dataset identification and causal/temporal design, the cell fate conclusions may be speculative.

The machine learning component is promising but underspecified. The proposal refers to contrastive multimodal embeddings, RNA-to-protein predictors, generative AI, vision foundation models, and biophysical constraints, but does not provide enough detail about model architectures, training/validation splits, avoidance of patient or section-level leakage, uncertainty quantification, interpretability, or external generalization. This is particularly important because spatial data are highly autocorrelated; random patch-level splits could produce inflated predictive accuracy. The proposal mentions leakage controls, but a stronger plan would explicitly require held-out patients, held-out tissues, held-out markers, and cross-platform validation. Similarly, the proposed biophysical features are plausible, but their relationship to mechanistic cell biology is not yet fully articulated. Terms such as 'biophysical fingerprint' and 'cell fate decision' need sharper operational definitions.

The project is well matched to NCEMS in its need for data harmonization, shared compute, project management, and open dissemination. It clearly uses existing public data and would benefit from a working group structure. Nonetheless, the proposal could more convincingly describe the broader community team, trainee participation, governance, and division of expertise. The requested resources are plausible, although the compute estimate appears imprecise, and the 24-month timeline is ambitious given the challenges of dataset harmonization, registration, model development, validation, application to additional cohorts, and manuscript/tool release.

Overall, this is a strong and relevant synthesis proposal with high potential to produce a useful community resource and to advance spatial omics integration. Its main limitations are the underdefinition of the application/fate datasets, possible overinterpretation of adjacent-section data as subcellular correspondence, and insufficiently detailed ML validation strategy. I would be enthusiastic if the project were framed primarily as a rigorous, open benchmarking and predictive integration framework for spatial RNA-protein cell-state analysis, with the cell fate component narrowed or made contingent on clearly identified public datasets with appropriate temporal or lineage information.

The proposed synthesis framework aims to integrate spatial transcriptomics (Xenium/CosMx) and spatial proteomics (CODEX) from adjacent tissue sections to create a 'biophysical fingerprint.' False correspondences could severely confound the machine learning models. We appreciate the inclusion of spatial shuffles as negative controls, but further strategies to filter noisy patches will be essential. Additionally, while the computational team is strong, developing, benchmarking, and validating generative AI models on terabytes of imaging data within the first 9-15 months is highly ambitious. 

The commitment to open science, specifically the release of containerized, reproducible workflows, is excellent and essential for the broader community to adopt these tools across diverse biological systems, including non-mammalian models.

Second, the computational request is exceptionally large (10^6 CPU and GPU hours); while training vision foundation models is intensive, the proposal needs a tighter justification for this exact scale, or a strategy for model checkpointing and efficient fine-tuning. While the 'Spatch' resource is excellently defined for Activities 1 and 2, the specific public datasets comprising the 'Application Set'—particularly those containing both required spatial modalities across a developmental or differentiation trajectory—are not clearly identified.
